title: Rényi Phase Transitions and Analytic Continuation to the von Neumann Entropy
authors: Ayush Raj, Akash Vijay, Hong-Chen Jiang, Laimei Nie
abstract: Extracting operationally meaningful quantities such as von Neumann entropy and mutual information is central to characterizing many-body quantum systems, yet experiments and numerics often provide direct access only to integer Rényi entropies. Whereas conventional extrapolation relies on a prescribed fitting ansatz, in PRL 137, 100202 we introduced an alternative approach based on stabilized analytic continuation (SAC), which avoids such an ansatz and is inherently robust to noise. Here, we further develop this framework in the noiseless setting and benchmark its performance across several nontrivial many-body problems. We first show that, besides the intrinsic ambiguity of reconstructing the von Neumann entropy from finitely many Rényi samples, analytic continuation can also fail because of genuine nonanalyticities in the Rényi function arising from zeros of $\text{Tr}ρ^z$. We derive universal zero-free domains for $\text{Tr}ρ^z$ and systematically sharpen these bounds using additional spectral information about $ρ$. We then benchmark the performance of SAC in three settings: ($i$) extracting topological entanglement entropy from DMRG Rényi data for the toric code and Kagome Heisenberg models; ($ii$) reconstructing the mutual information between disjoint intervals in a $(1+1)d$ compact-boson CFT; and ($iii$) recovering finite-time ballistic growth of the von Neumann entropy from integer Rényi entropies that cross over toward subballistic growth in diffusive quantum dynamics. In the latter setting, analytic continuation is expected to fail in the long time limit. We illustrate this mechanism with a physically motivated two-sector model, where the asymptotic separation between von Neumann and higher-Rényi growth is accompanied by a zero of $\text{Tr}ρ^z$ pinching the real axis at $z=1$, thereby producing a first-order Rényi phase transition.
summary: This paper presents Stabilized Analytic Continuation (SAC) as a robust method to calculate the von Neumann entropy from limited integer Rényi entropy measurements. The authors provide deep theoretical insights into the limitations of this process, particularly identifying how zeros of the trace function $	ext{Tr} ho^z$ can cause analytic continuation to fail, leading to observable phase transitions.
main_problem: The central challenge is extracting the physically meaningful von Neumann entropy ($S_{	ext{vN}}$) from numerical data that only provides access to integer Rényi entropies ($S_n$).
main_result: The authors developed and rigorously analyzed Stabilized Analytic Continuation (SAC), showing it is robust but can fail when the Rényi function develops singularities (Fisher zeros) due to zeros of $	ext{Tr} ho^z$.
method: The work combines analytic continuation techniques, mapping the problem onto a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) framework, and deriving universal bounds on the location of singularities based on spectral properties.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to general many-body quantum systems, benchmarking performance on the toric code, Kagome Heisenberg models, and $(1+1)d$ compact-boson CFTs.
key_observables: Von Neumann entropy ($S_{	ext{vN}}$), mutual information, integer Rényi entropies ($S_n$), and the function $	ext{Tr} ho^z$ in the complex $z$-plane.
important_parameters: The rank ($r$) of the density matrix, the number of input Rényi samples ($N$), and the location of zeros of $	ext{Tr} ho^z$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes a noiseless setting for the theoretical derivations, and the SAC method relies on the minimum-norm interpolant within a specific RKHS structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SAC construction, the extraction of topological entanglement entropy for the Kagome model, and the reconstruction of mutual information across various physical benchmarks.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces SAC as a robust alternative to conventional extrapolation. It then provides theoretical derivations establishing zero-free domains for $	ext{Tr} ho^z$ and deriving bounds on singularities. Finally, it benchmarks SAC performance across three distinct physical settings: topological entropy, mutual information, and quantum dynamics.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework connecting entanglement entropy calculation to complex analysis (RKHS theory) provides powerful, general tools for analyzing quantum correlations in strongly correlated systems.

The semi-infinite strip {Re z ≥1, | Im z| ≤ϵ} is mapped to the upper half-plane by ξ = i sinh[π(z −1)/(2ϵ)], and subsequently to the unit disc by w = (ξ −iη)/(ξ + iη).
